issues.legal_issue: In a contract for the sale of immovable property, fixing completion dates and providing for a penalty do not by themselves make time essential.
material_facts: The parties orally agreed to sell a plot of land without fixing a completion date, then made written agreements fixing completion dates and providing for a penalty if either party failed to complete the sale.
The agreements did not state in unmistakable terms that time was essential.
Although the sellers urgently needed money, the circumstances did not show that the parties intended time to be essential.
issues.conclusion: Time was not of the essence of the contract.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 55 of the Contract Act, 1872, failure to perform by a specified time makes a contract voidable for that reason only if the parties intended time to be essential. In a sale of immovable property, time is ordinarily presumed not to be essential; that presumption may be displaced by unmistakable express language or sufficiently strong circumstances. Fixing a completion date or including a penalty clause is not, by itself, enough. The court relied on Jamshed Khodaram Irani v. Burjorji Dhunjibhai and Stickney v. Keeble.

predicates.contract_for_land_sale: The parties agreed to sell immovable property under a contract.
predicates.no_unmistakable_time_term: The contract did not express in unmistakable terms that the parties intended time to be essential.
predicates.no_strong_circumstances_making_time_esse: The circumstances surrounding the contract were not sufficiently strong to show that the parties intended time to be essential.

issues.definition: When the parties agreed to sell immovable property and neither unmistakable terms nor sufficiently strong circumstances show that they intended time to be essential, time is not essential.

issues.legal_issue: When time is not essential to a contract for the sale of land, delay alone does not establish default unless the other party gives notice requiring completion within a reasonable time.
material_facts: Time was not of the essence of the agreement.
The sellers did not give notice fixing a reasonable time for the purchaser to complete the sale.
The sellers instead sent a letter treating the agreement as cancelled, and the purchaser had delayed calling for completion.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser's delay in calling for completion did not, by itself, establish default; the sellers' cancellation letter did not determine the purchaser's right to specific performance on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Where time was not originally of the essence, default cannot be inferred merely from delay. A party seeking to bring the contract to an end must give notice requiring completion within a reasonable fixed time and the other party must fail to comply. The court relied on section 55 of the Contract Act, 1872, and Stickney v. Keeble.

predicates.contract_did_not_make_time_essential: The parties' contract did not make timely completion essential.
predicates.other_party_gave_no_reasonable_completio: The other contracting party did not give notice requiring completion within a reasonable time.
predicates.delay_occurred: The party required to complete the contract delayed taking steps to do so.

issues.definition: If time was not essential, the other party gave no reasonable completion notice, and delay occurred, the delay alone is not default.

issues.legal_issue: A claimant seeking specific performance must prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform the contract, and an unoverturned finding that this requirement was not met prevents a decree.
material_facts: The purchaser sought specific performance and pleaded that he had always been ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
The trial court found, based on the purchaser's evidence and conduct, that he was not ready and willing to perform his part of the contract.
That finding was not challenged before the High Court, and the High Court did not hold it to be incorrect.
The Supreme Court accepted the trial court's finding and held that the High Court could not grant specific performance without setting it aside.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was not entitled to specific performance, and the trial court's dismissal of the suit was restored.
issues.legal_principle: A claimant seeking specific performance must plead and prove continuous readiness and willingness to perform from the date of the contract until the hearing; failure to establish this requires dismissal of the claim. The court relied on Ardeshir Mamna v. Flora Sassoon. It also held that the trial court's adverse finding could not be disregarded without considering the evidence and setting the finding aside.

predicates.specific_performance_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking specific performance of a contract.
predicates.claimant_not_continuously_ready: The claimant did not establish continuous readiness and willingness to perform the claimant's part of the contract.
predicates.adverse_readiness_finding_not_overturned: The trial court found against the claimant on readiness and willingness, and that finding was not set aside on appeal.

issues.definition: In a specific-performance suit, if the claimant was not continuously ready and willing and the adverse trial finding remains unoverturned, specific performance must be denied.
